prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: focal neurological signs (left extensor plantar response, left facial droop, asymmetric limb weakness) are an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 Annex A.4.
Do not rely on ampicillin to treat the Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate (intrinsic resistance): it is empirical Listeria cover only and is stopped once Klebsiella is identified.
Do not interpret the CSF glucose without the paired blood glucose: in hyperglycaemia the ratio, not the absolute value, is decisive; here 8 over 312 gives 0.026.
Do NOT withhold ceftriaxone or ampicillin solely because of a reported childhood penicillin rash: he has since tolerated repeated amoxicillin courses, and cephalosporin cross-reactivity is low.
Do NOT treat with shorter than 21-day IV antibiotic course for Gram-negative bacillary meningitis.
Do NOT continue metformin in acute illness with creatinine elevation and sepsis (risk of lactic acidosis).
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6); the reported childhood penicillin rash does not preclude it, since he has since tolerated repeated amoxicillin courses.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Stop dexamethasone on identification of Klebsiella pneumoniae (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because focal neurological signs are present (left extensor plantar response, left facial droop, asymmetric limb weakness) (WHO 2025 Annex A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (opening pressure, cell count with differential, glucose with simultaneous blood glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR panel, CSF lactate) at the LP.
Interpret CSF glucose as the CSF:blood ratio: in hyperglycaemia the ratio, not the absolute value, is decisive; here 8 over 312 gives 0.026.

Obtain contrast-enhanced MRI brain with MR venography to exclude subdural or epidural empyema, brain abscess and sigmoid or transverse sinus thrombosis complicating two weeks of left otomastoiditis with focal neurological signs.
Withhold metformin (sepsis, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL) and glipizide during the acute illness; control glucose with insulin and close monitoring while on dexamethasone.
Place patient in droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours for the ceftriaxone-susceptible Klebsiella pneumoniae, stopping ampicillin, for 21 days, the usual duration for Gram-negative bacillary meningitis; meropenem if an ESBL-producing isolate is reported.
Urgent ENT assessment for surgical drainage of the left otomastoiditis source (myringotomy with or without mastoidectomy).
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, and within 4 weeks of being well enough to test (NICE NG240).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis; sinus tachycardia in this context is a non-specific finding of infection/fever.
No evidence of endocarditis as a source; bacteremia arises from the otomastoid focus. Echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup without endocarditis features.
No arrhythmia indication; sinus tachycardia in the setting of sepsis/fever does not require cardiac monitoring workup.
PET imaging has no role in acute bacterial meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover all imaging indications.

key_clinical_evidence: A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value: in hyperglycaemia the ratio, not the absolute value, is decisive; here 8 over 312 gives 0.026.

Gram-negative bacillary meningitis (Enterobacterales, including Klebsiella) is an uncommon cause of community-acquired meningitis, associated with diabetes mellitus and with head-and-neck infections such as otomastoiditis.
A negative multiplex panel never excludes Gram-negative bacillary meningitis: Enterobacterales other than E. coli K1 are not panel targets, and culture establishes the organism.

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025). Diabetes is counted as a Listeria risk factor in this benchmark.

Klebsiella pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to ampicillin: empirical ampicillin is Listeria cover, not treatment of the isolate, and is stopped once Klebsiella is identified; targeted therapy follows the susceptibilities (ceftriaxone here, meropenem if an ESBL producer).
A reported childhood penicillin rash followed by tolerated amoxicillin courses is a low-risk label; it does not preclude ampicillin or ceftriaxone in life-threatening infection.
Gram-negative bacillary meningitis is usually treated for 21 days, longer than the NICE NG240 durations for pneumococcal (14 days) or meningococcal (5 days) meningitis.
Two weeks of otomastoiditis with focal neurological signs require contrast-enhanced MRI with venography: a non-contrast CT cannot exclude subdural empyema, brain abscess or sigmoid sinus thrombosis.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because focal neurological signs are present (WHO 2025 Annex A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

red_herrings.intended_effect: Prompt the agent to avoid ceftriaxone and ampicillin and substitute an inferior regimen (e.g., vancomycin alone, or omission of Listeria cover).

The neutrophilic CSF with a glucose ratio of 0.026 remains bacterial meningitis until culture identifies the organism (Klebsiella pneumoniae).

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 Annex A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilloedema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. NICE NG240 1.4.7 agrees (new focal neurological features). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: Gram-negative bacillary meningitis mimicking an ENT primary diagnosis; negative initial Gram stain; CSF glucose interpretation complicated by severe hyperglycemia; reported penicillin allergy complicating empiric antibiotic selection. Four grounded red herrings. Requires 7 required tools plus synthesis of CSF:serum ratio, allergy risk stratification, and organism-appropriate antibiotic duration.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Carlos Mendez is a 54-year-old right-handed Hispanic man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and a history of recurrent bilateral otitis media who presents to the emergency department brought by his wife via EMS after she found him increasingly difficult to arouse this morning.

Per his wife, Mr. Mendez began complaining approximately two weeks ago of severe left ear pain and bilateral fullness in the ears, initially attributed by her to his chronic ear problems. He had a low-grade fever at home measured at 38.1 degrees Celsius on the first day and was seen by his primary care physician six days ago, who prescribed a course of amoxicillin for presumed acute otitis media. Despite the amoxicillin, he developed worsening headache — diffuse, severe, pressure-like, rated 9 out of 10 — that was not relieved by over-the-counter analgesics. He discontinued the amoxicillin on his own after two days because of gastrointestinal side effects and did not return for follow-up.

Over the past 5 days, his wife noticed progressive confusion: he was forgetting appointments, repeating himself, and seemed generally 'not himself.' She attributed his confusion to poor sleep and poor glycemic control, as he had not been monitoring his blood sugars closely. Yesterday evening he became more lethargic, declining dinner and going to bed early. This morning he was arousable only to loud voice, and she was unable to get him to recognize where he was. He complained briefly of neck pain before becoming less communicative. She activated EMS.

He denies — per remote history and prior notes — any recent neurosurgical procedures, lumbar punctures, or CSF shunts. He has no history of prior meningitis, encephalitis, or stroke. He has no known HIV status but has no documented risk factors per his wife. He has not taken any antibiotics beyond the brief amoxicillin course. He has not traveled internationally in the past three years. No pets at home. No sick contacts with meningitis-like illness. His wife reports that his blood sugars have been running high — she recalls a reading of 320 mg/dL two days ago.

neurological_exam.additional: Nuchal rigidity present with marked resistance to passive neck flexion. Kernig sign positive bilaterally. Brudzinski sign positive. Left tympanic membrane opaque with loss of light reflex on otoscopic exam; mucopurulent discharge visible in the left external auditory canal. Right tympanic membrane dull with mild retraction. No petechiae, purpura, or rash on full skin examination. No lymphadenopathy.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to assess reliably due to altered mental status.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4 mm bilaterally, equally reactive to light (sluggish). No papilledema appreciated on limited fundoscopic exam. Rightward gaze preference, overcome by the oculocephalic manoeuvre; no gaze palsy. Mild left facial droop at the nasolabial fold, symmetric activation to painful stimulation. Hearing grossly reduced bilaterally, worse on the left by whisper test. Gag reflex present. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to assess; patient transported to ED by EMS on stretcher.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Drowsy but arousable to voice. Oriented to name only; unable to state the date or location. Responds to simple commands inconsistently. Speech is slow and dysarthric when the patient responds. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Unable to complete formal cognitive testing.
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all four extremities to painful stimulation. Right upper and lower extremity strength estimated 4+/5. Left upper extremity 4/5, left lower extremity 4/5. Tone mildly increased bilaterally. No pronator drift assessable. No visible fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Left plantar response extensor (Babinski positive). Right plantar response flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws to pain symmetrically in all four extremities. Detailed sensory examination not possible.
